classification_signals: The paper describes a field study involving measurements of roadside noise levels at two sites (p. 2). It details the 'Method' (p. 2), 'Analysis' (p. 6), and 'Results' (p. 6) sections. The methodology includes 'carefully controlled measurement conditions' (p. 1 abstract) and a 'before and after' design where barrier panels were reversed (p. 2, p. 6). Statistical methods like 'multiple regression' and 'analysis of variance' were used (p. 6), and results are presented in tables with p-values (confidence limits) and effect sizes (dB changes) (p. 7, 9).
title: Effects on roadside noise levels of sound absorptive materials in noise barriers

limitations: Further carefully controlled field studies with varying traffic flows are required to fully quantify the effects of vehicle flow in scattering sound and site parameters such as the barrier separation to height ratio.
The CRTN prediction model has limitations including simplified geometry, no account of vehicle-barrier reflections behind the barrier, and no consideration of traffic scattering effects.
The actual reflective properties of large vehicles may not provide conditions for specular reflections, potentially explaining the lack of significant changes in LA1.
Less than perfect absorption and reflective properties of the barrier panels themselves may slightly reduce the observed noise level increases compared to ideal conditions.

Simplified geometry assumptions in prediction models, such as the presence of safety fences, reflective ground beams, and limited barrier length/curvature, may have reduced the measured noise increases.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical field study investigated the effects of sound absorptive materials in roadside noise barriers on noise levels. Researchers measured A-weighted noise levels at two sites (motorway and dual carriageway) before and after reversing barrier panels to change their traffic-facing side from absorptive to reflective. Key findings indicate that changing the barrier face from absorptive to reflective generally resulted in an increase of roadside noise levels, typically less than 1 dB, though some specific receiver positions showed increases up to 2.28 dB (LAeq) and 2.09 dB (LA10) at the dual carriageway site with parallel reflective barriers. The study found that UK traffic noise prediction models (CRTN) tended to overestimate these noise increases compared to measured values, particularly at greater distances from the barrier. Limitations include the need for further studies on varying traffic flows and site parameters, and the simplified geometry and assumptions about traffic scattering and material properties in current prediction models.
